title: Satisfiability of full MSO+U over infinite words
formal: Is satisfiability of full monadic second-order logic with the unbounding quantifier, \(\mathrm{MSO}+U\), decidable over infinite words? Precisely, is there a single deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite input consisting of a finite alphabet and an \(\mathrm{MSO}+U\) sentence, and answers YES exactly when some infinite word over that alphabet satisfies the sentence? The selected 2012 source question concerns full set quantification; the imported title incorrectly inserted “weak.”

source_formulation.text: It is an open problem whether satisfiability is decidable over infinite words.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 1

why: Monadic logic over infinite words is a basic language for reasoning about infinite behavior. The unbounding quantifier expresses that finite patterns can grow without limit. Classifying its interaction with unrestricted set quantification identifies a fundamental boundary between decidable specifications and undecidable ones.
status_note: Resolved negatively by Bojańczyk–Parys–Toruńczyk, STACS 2016: full MSO+U satisfiability over infinite words is undecidable without extra set-theoretic hypotheses. The source question was mislabelled weak in the import; the weak fragment is separately decidable. The corrected full source question and all original provenance are retained in the archive.

importance.reason: This settles a natural expressiveness-versus-decidability boundary for monadic logic over infinite words: the weak extension is decidable, while unrestricted set quantification with unbounding is not. The result connects automata, infinite structures and logical undecidability and resolves the source’s explicitly stated question.

sentences: Full monadic second-order logic over an infinite word can quantify over arbitrary sets of positions.
The unbounding quantifier says that a property holds for finite sets of arbitrarily large size.
The original source asks whether satisfiability remains decidable when these forms of quantification interact without restrictions.
The imported title mistakenly named the weaker finite-set fragment.
The corrected full-logic question was resolved negatively by the unconditional 2016 undecidability theorem.

definitions: An alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{1,\ldots,a\}\) for an input integer \(a\ge1\). An infinite word is a function \(w:\mathbb N\to\Sigma\), interpreted as a structure with domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), the usual strict order \(<\), and unary predicates \(P_b(t)\) meaning \(w(t)=b\), for each \(b\in\Sigma\). First-order variables range over positions \(t\in\mathbb N\). Monadic second-order variables range over arbitrary subsets of \(\mathbb N\), including infinite subsets. Atomic formulas are \(x=y\), \(x<y\), \(x\in X\) and \(P_b(x)\). Formulas are generated by these atoms, Boolean connectives, first-order and monadic second-order existential quantifiers, and the unbounding quantifier \(UX\,\varphi\); universal quantifiers may be expressed through negation and existential quantification. Nesting of quantifiers and use of negation are unrestricted. With all other free variables held at their assigned values, \[w\models UX\,\varphi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall k\in\mathbb N\ \exists F\subseteq\mathbb N:\ F\text{ is finite},\ |F|\ge k,\ \text{and }w\models\varphi[X:=F].\] Thus the variable bound by \(U\) is interpreted by arbitrarily large finite sets, even though ordinary second-order quantifiers range over all sets. A sentence has no free variables. It is satisfiable if there exists any infinite word \(w\) satisfying it under these full semantics; the word need not be periodic, computable or supplied as input. Encode \(a\), variable and letter indices, connectives and the finite formula parse tree by a fixed effective binary encoding. Invalid encodings are rejected. Decidable means that one finite deterministic Turing-machine program returns the correct Boolean answer and halts on every input, with no required upper bound on running time or memory. It has no oracle, advice or access to an infinite witness word. The weak variant \(\mathrm{WMSO}+U\) restricts ordinary set quantifiers to finite sets and is a different logic.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that a total decision algorithm exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A positive answer must cover every input alphabet and sentence with unrestricted nesting and full set quantification. A negative answer must establish undecidability under the stated standard semantics; undecidability of a different logic, an infinite-tree result alone, or an argument conditional on an extra set-theoretic hypothesis does not suffice. The known published answer to this source question is negative.

context_blocks.text: The sentence selected from the 2012 introduction refers to full MSO+U. The title of that paper concerns the weak fragment, and its main theorem proves a decidability result for that fragment. The imported card confused the paper’s subject with the logic in its quoted open question.

In the weak fragment, ordinary set variables are restricted to finite sets. The 2012 discussion explicitly distinguishes this fragment from full MSO+U and records the decidability of its infinite-word satisfiability problem.

Bojańczyk, Parys and Toruńczyk prove in their 2016 Theorem 1.1 that the full MSO+U theory of the natural-number order is undecidable. Their Section 3 also directly establishes undecidability of satisfiability on infinite words over a finite alphabet, matching this question.
The 2016 result uses no additional set-theoretic assumption. It therefore strengthens earlier conditional results about full MSO+U on infinite trees and resolves the 2012 infinite-word question.
